title: Two bowls, swapped
hook: two bowls swapped in a kitchen, and a family of sages raises a fighter
carry: svadharma: your dharma follows your nature
tomorrow: his father gives an order no son should get. what does he do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third stride landed on Bali's bowed head, and Vishnu promised to guard his door: atma-nivedana, offering yourself, not just your things. Now the next form in the row, and this one carries an axe.

Somebody grabs the wrong coffee cup. Here's an older version. Parashurama is a sage's son who carries a warrior's axe, and in the world of these stories that's strange: priests study, warriors fight. The Bhagavata explains it with a mix-up in a kitchen. Two bowls of blessed rice pudding, one for a priest's calm, one for a warrior's fire. And the two women they were meant for swap them.
screen: `SOMEBODY GRABS THE WRONG CUP.` → `A SAGE'S SON WITH AN AXE.` → `TWO BOWLS, SWAPPED.`

segments.voice: The sage Richika blesses two portions: one for his wife, Satyavati, to bear a son with a priest's calm; one for her mother, to bear a son with a warrior's fire. Her mother guesses a husband would bless his own wife's bowl best, and talks her daughter into a swap. When Richika finds out, he tells Satyavati what it means: her son will be fierce. She pleads, and he grants this much: the fire will skip a generation. So her son, Jamadagni, grows up a calm and learned sage. And Jamadagni's son, with his wife Renuka, is the one who carries the fire. That's Parashurama. His name puts parashu, an axe, beside the name Rama; tradition says Shiva gave him the axe. And the other bowl? Many tellings say it went the other way: Satyavati's brother, Vishvamitra, was born a king and became one of the greatest sages. So what were the bowls carrying? A nature. Old Hindu thought names four callings, the varnas: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, traders, and workers. In the Gita, Krishna says those callings follow guna and karma, a person's qualities and their work, and that it's better to live your own dharma, svadharma, imperfectly than someone else's well. For centuries, varna was mostly fixed by birth and hardened into caste, which many Hindu teachers have challenged. Many readers hear this story as a door left open: a sage's son with a warrior's fire, a king's son who becomes a sage. And today? When a family says 'we're all doctors' and a kid has a firefighter's fire, the Gita's question isn't 'what's your family name?' It's 'what's your nature, and what work will you do with it?'
screen: `TWO PORTIONS: CALM AND FIRE.` · `THE FIRE SKIPS A GENERATION.` · `VISHVAMITRA: THE KING WHO BECAME A SAGE.` · `GUNA AND KARMA: NATURE AND WORK.` · then, large: `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, as steady as someone keeping watch, and let the breath go calm and even underneath: the warrior in the spine, the sage in the breath. Many Vishnu devotees repeat a short name on each breath: Om Namo Narayanaya. Say it silently for a few rounds. If you don't pray, just keep the two together, alert and quiet. Near the end, ask: what is my own dharma?
Parashurama: Rama with the axe, Vishnu's form as a sage's son born with a warrior's fire.
Your line: svadharma, your dharma follows your nature. Two bowls swapped, and sages raised a fighter. See you tomorrow.
